title: Can it fit a whole chicken? The two measurements that answer it, before you order
desc: Quarts do not tell you whether a bird fits. What does: the cavity you can actually use and the 165°F check you have to be able to make inside it. Capacity, footprint and food safety across three air fryers.
image_caption: Editorial illustration of an oven-style fryer with a whole bird on the rack. Not a product photograph, and not a fit guarantee.
body:
“Will it take a whole chicken?” is the question that turns an air-fryer browse into a decision, and the capacity number in the product name is the wrong place to answer it. Two measurements settle it — one you take off a listing, one you take off your own bird with a tape measure.

1. What the listings on this shelf actually state

ProductCapacity, as listedExterior footprint, as listedWeight, as listed
Chefman 6 Qt Dual Basket6 Quart, described as two independent 3-Qt baskets13.38"D x 11.81"W x 10.63"H13.3 pounds
Chefman 8 Qt TurboFry8 Quarts, one XL basket12.75"D x 13.5"W x 10"H12.8 Pounds
Emeril Lagasse 26QT French Door26QT (24.6 Liters), oven-style cavity16.9"D x 15.8"W x 14.8"H26.5 Pounds

Read the third column carefully: those are the exterior dimensions the listings publish. None of the three states an interior cavity measurement, so the usable space is always smaller than the box you are comparing to your shelf. That is the number to chase down on the manufacturer's spec sheet before you buy — not to guess at.

Sources: Chefman 6 Qt Dual Basket · Chefman 8 Qt TurboFry · Emeril 26QT French Door · read 2026-11-20.

2. One seller's claim, quoted as a claim

The Emeril listing's own bullet copy states a 6-lb chicken on the rotisserie and a 12" pizza. That is a seller's figure, recorded here because it is checkable on the page — not a measurement this site made, and not a promise about your bird. Where a listing contradicts itself (the same page says “Six Cooking Accessories Included” in the title and lists seven in the bullets, and 24 presets in the title against 25 in the bullets), this site publishes both readings and flags them instead of picking a side — see the flag register.

Sources: Emeril 26QT listing (accessory and preset counts both appear) · read 2026-11-20.

3. The food-safety half, which decides the size

A bird is only done when it is done. USDA FSIS cooks all poultry to a minimum internal temperature of 165°F, and for a whole bird says to check the internal temperature in three places: the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing, and the thickest part of the breast, avoiding bone. If you stuff the bird, the centre of the stuffing must also reach 165°F — and FSIS adds that for optimum safety you should not stuff whole poultry at all.

Now look at those three check points in a basket that is 10 inches tall with a basket inside it. If your hand cannot get a thermometer into the thigh and the wing without negotiating the basket wall or burning your knuckles, the appliance is the wrong size regardless of how the bird fits. This is the constraint that quietly rules out more machines than capacity does.

Food-safety sources: USDA FSIS — Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart · USDA FSIS — Food Thermometers · read 2026-11-20.

4. Basket shape changes the answer, not just the volume

  • Two 3-quart baskets — a whole bird does not go in one of them as a bird. This shape is for two different foods finishing together, which is why the listing pairs it with a Sync Finish feature.
  • One 8-quart basket — a wide single layer; a bird has to lie flat, and pieces, thighs and spatchcocked halves are what this shape is genuinely good for.
  • 26QT oven cavity with doors — the only shape on this shelf with vertical clearance and a rack, and it costs 16.9 inches of counter depth and 26.5 pounds of permanence.

Nothing above is a judgement about which is better. It is geometry: the listed dimensions either leave room for a bird and a thermometer hand, or they do not.

A three-minute way to settle it before you buy

  1. Measure your usual bird (or the piece you cook most) at its widest and tallest points with a tape.
  2. Take the exterior numbers off the listing and subtract a wall allowance — you are buying interior space, and no listing on this shelf publishes it.
  3. Check you can reach three places on the bird with a thermometer while the basket or door is open.
  4. Confirm the counter depth where the unit will live permanently, and that the outlet is reachable without an adapter cord.
What this page will not do. It states no cooking times, no “juiciest bird” claim and no test result, because nobody here has roasted a chicken in any of these units. The appliance numbers are copied from the listings; the temperature and placement rules are USDA FSIS’s. No prices appear on this site — Amazon’s Program Policies keep price display on Amazon’s own served pages.

The three air fryers on this shelf

CARDS
faq: Can you cook a whole chicken in a 6-quart air fryer?

Not as a bird in this shelf's 6-quart machine — that capacity is delivered as two independent 3-quart baskets, which is a shape for cooking two things at once rather than one large object. Check the listing's own basket description before assuming a single cavity.
What temperature is a whole chicken done to?

USDA FSIS sets a minimum internal temperature of 165°F for all poultry, including a whole bird. For a whole bird, check three places — the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing and the thickest part of the breast, avoiding bone. If you stuff it, the centre of the stuffing must also reach 165°F; FSIS adds that for optimum safety you should not stuff whole poultry.
Does a 26-quart oven-style air fryer need more counter space than a basket model?

By the listed numbers, yes: the 26QT French-door unit is listed at 16.9"D x 15.8"W x 14.8"H and 26.5 pounds, against 13.38"D x 11.81"W x 10.63"H at 13.3 pounds for the twin-basket unit and 12.75"D x 13.5"W x 10"H at 12.8 pounds for the 8-quart. Those are exterior dimensions, so clearance around the unit is extra.
Why doesn't this page give a chicken cooking time?

Because a time would be a claim with no source. Nothing on the listings has been measured by this site, and a safe poultry result is defined by the internal temperature USDA FSIS publishes (165°F), verified with a thermometer in three places — not by minutes per pound.
